overview: The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies formally united Naples and Sicily in 1816. This map label starts earlier, so the card also explains achievements under the preceding Bourbon crowns and the separate Napoleonic government on the mainland. The unified kingdom combined major scientific and industrial projects with political repression and repeated revolutions.

periods.title: Two Bourbon crowns
periods.summary: Naples and Sicily shared rulers before their formal constitutional union.

periods.title: Divided by the Napoleonic wars
periods.summary: The mainland experienced French dynastic government while the Bourbon monarchy retained Sicily.

periods.title: The united kingdom
periods.summary: The 1816 union was followed by revolution, repression and conquest during Italian unification.

items.text: At San Leucio near Caserta, silk machinery was installed in the 1780s with help from foreign specialists. The royal industrial settlement predates the formal 1816 kingdom. It linked imported expertise with the daily work of spinning and weaving luxurious cloth.

The settlement’s 1789 code required education and regulated work and pay. It also abolished dowries within the community and prescribed uniform clothing. These were rules for a particular royal colony, not evidence that every woman and child across southern Italy enjoyed the same conditions.

San Leucio’s rules included mutual assistance for elderly people and those unable to work. The planned expansion into Ferdinandopoli, however, was never completed as intended. Reforming a small community on paper and transforming an entire society were very different scales of ambition.

The silk works depended on a branch of the Carolino aqueduct. After driving production, water returned to the Peschiera basin. The same royal landscape joined useful machinery and ornamental water: a beautiful fountain view could be connected to a working industrial system.

Maria Carolina’s rooms at Caserta preserve a bidet, dressing table and bathtub among the furnishings studied by the museum. These objects make royal washing arrangements tangible. They are evidence for an elite interior, not a census of ordinary families’ plumbing.

Palermo’s larger botanical garden was established from 1789 and inaugurated in 1795. Bernardino da Ucria arranged its collections using Linnaeus’s classification. Plants were being organized as teaching material, while the garden’s buildings provided spaces for study and cultivation.

On 1 January 1801, Giuseppe Piazzi observed the object now called Ceres from Palermo. Further observations showed its movement, and Gauss later helped calculate its orbit. Now classified as a dwarf planet, Ceres connects Sicilian observation with an international mathematical effort.

Naples’s Capodimonte observatory began under Joachim Murat in 1812 and was completed under Ferdinand I in 1819. The project crossed a change of regime. Its history is a useful reminder that an institution’s achievements cannot always be assigned neatly to one dynasty.

The Naples to Portici railway opened on 3 October 1839. Its roughly 7.4-kilometre inaugural journey took about eleven minutes. It was a short route, but a real change in transport; the engineering drew on British locomotive designs and the work of Armand Bayard.

In 1840 the crown began acquiring land for the Pietrarsa works. The surviving factory halls housed specialized stages of production and now contain railway collections. A steam railway required a continuing workforce and repair capacity, not just a ceremonial first ride.

sections.title: Political limits and a written voice

items.text: Revolutions in 1820 and 1848 forced concessions before royal power reasserted itself. Sicilian demands for independence also conflicted with control from Naples. These struggles explain why scientific projects and royal factories could coexist with fierce opposition to the monarchy.

Italian, Giuseppe Piazzi’s words reproduced by INAF from his historical record: “non vi essendo Cielo più bello del Partenopeo”. Translation: “there being no sky more beautiful than Naples’s.” The phrase belongs to his discussion of Naples and its observatory. The exhibition does not date this individual quotation, so an exact year would be misleading.

ending.text: Garibaldi’s campaign and Piedmontese intervention brought annexation in 1860. The Bourbon court’s last major stand at Gaeta ended on 13 February 1861, and the territory entered the new Kingdom of Italy. Resistance and social conflict continued afterward; this was the end of a state, not of southern Italian communities.
